issues.legal_issue: A suit challenging a finding made by a public officer in the discharge of official duties requires prior notice when the officer is sued in that official capacity.
material_facts: The respondent sued the State and the Registrar to set aside the Registrar’s finding that a religious institution was a public trust.
The Registrar made the finding in the performance of official duties under the public-trust registration scheme.
The respondent did not serve notice before filing the suit.
The trial court dismissed the suit for want of notice, but the High Court held that notice was unnecessary.
issues.conclusion: Notice was required because the suit sought to set aside an order made by a public officer in the discharge of official duties; the High Court’s judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure is express, explicit, and mandatory, and applies to a suit against a public officer in respect of an act purporting to be done in official capacity. Such acts include non-feasance and illegal omissions, and the rule does not distinguish between acts done illegally or in bad faith and those done bona fide. The Court relied on Sawai Singhai Nirmal Chand v. Union of India, Bhagchand Dagadusa v. Secretary of State for India in Council, and Prasaddas v. Bennerjee.

predicates.public_trust_finding_suit: A person brings a civil suit challenging a finding about whether a trust is public.
predicates.official_capacity_order: A public officer made the challenged finding while performing official duties.
predicates.notice_not_served: The person bringing the suit did not give the required prior notice to the government or public officer.
predicates.suit_is_not_maintainable_without_require: The suit cannot proceed because the required prior notice was not given.

issues.definition: When a person challenges a public-trust finding made by a public officer in an official capacity and gives no required prior notice, the suit cannot proceed.
